title: Paxos Simplified
description: Walk through single-decree Paxos step by step: proposers, acceptors, learners, majority quorums, and why it's notoriously hard to implement correctly.

segments.text: Paxos is the grandfather of consensus algorithms. Published by Leslie Lamport in 1998, it's been called 'the only consensus protocol' by some researchers. It's also been called 'impossible to understand' by engineers who've tried to implement it. Today, I'll make it click. No Greek parliament metaphors. Just the actual protocol.

The problem: multiple nodes need to agree on a single value, even if some nodes crash, messages get delayed, or messages arrive out of order. We can't use a single leader because the leader might crash. We need an algorithm where any node can propose a value and the group reliably agrees on exactly one.

Three roles in Paxos. Proposers suggest values. Acceptors vote on proposals. Learners discover the decided value. In practice, every node plays all three roles simultaneously. A majority quorum is any set of more than half the acceptors. With five acceptors, you need three. Any two majorities overlap by at least one node, which is the key insight.

Phase one: Prepare. A proposer picks a unique proposal number, say n equals 42, and sends Prepare of 42 to all acceptors. Each acceptor checks: is 42 higher than any proposal number I've seen before? If yes, it promises to never accept proposals with numbers lower than 42, and replies with any value it has already accepted.

Phase two: Accept. Once the proposer receives promises from a majority, it sends Accept of 42 with a value. Here's the crucial rule: if any acceptor already accepted a value in its promise response, the proposer must use the value from the highest-numbered accepted proposal. It can't just use its own value. This constraint is what makes Paxos safe.
segments.thought_prompt: Why must the proposer adopt an already-accepted value instead of using its own?

segments.text: When a majority of acceptors accept the same proposal, the value is decided. Learners detect this by observing acceptor responses. Once decided, no other value can ever be decided, even if new proposals come in. They'll be forced to adopt the already-decided value through the prepare phase. That's the safety guarantee.

But Paxos has a liveness problem. Two proposers can duel forever. Proposer A sends Prepare of 1, gets promises. Before A can send Accept, Proposer B sends Prepare of 2, invalidating A's promises. A retries with Prepare of 3, invalidating B. This livelock can theoretically continue indefinitely. In practice, randomized backoff solves it.

Why is Paxos hard to implement? Single-decree Paxos decides one value. Real systems need to decide a sequence of values, a replicated log. Multi-Paxos extends the protocol but Lamport's paper left many practical details unspecified: leader election, log compaction, membership changes. Every implementation fills these gaps differently and usually incorrectly the first time.

Google's Chubby lock service used Paxos internally and the team famously described it as 'surprisingly difficult.' The paper on Chubby states there's a significant gap between the Paxos description and the needs of a real-world system. This frustration directly inspired the creation of Raft, which we'll cover in the next lesson.
segments.thought_prompt: If Paxos is so hard, why don't we just use a simpler protocol? What would we lose?

segments.text: Paxos matters because it proves consensus is possible in an asynchronous system with crash failures. It's the theoretical foundation. You may never implement Paxos directly, but understanding prepare-accept phases and majority quorums is essential for grasping every consensus system you'll encounter: Raft, ZAB, Viewstamped Replication, all of them.
